title: The Impact of Legalized Abortion on Crime
research_question: Did the legalization of abortion in the United States in the early 1970s contribute to the substantial decline in crime rates observed in the 1990s? If so, through what magnitude and mechanisms (cohort size reductions versus reductions in per-capita offending among affected cohorts) does access to abortion translate into lower subsequent criminal activity?
data_description: The analysis combines several U.S. data sources at the state-year level for roughly 1973-1997. Crime data (violent crime, property crime, and murder rates per capita) come from the FBI's Uniform Crime Reports, supplemented by the National Crime Victimization Survey for national trends. Arrest data, broken down by single year of age (15-24) and by broader age groups, also come from the UCR for 1985-1996. Abortion counts and rates per 1000 live births by state are taken from the Alan Guttmacher Institute. The authors construct an 'effective abortion rate' that weights past state abortion rates by the age distribution of arrestees. State-level controls include prisoners and police per capita, personal income per capita, unemployment rate, poverty rate, lagged AFDC generosity, concealed-handgun laws, beer consumption, and immigrant flows. The unit of observation is the state-year (50 states plus DC).
institutional_context: Abortion was illegal throughout the United States by 1900 and remained so until a wave of liberalization beginning in 1967. Five states—Alaska, California, Hawaii, New York, and Washington—repealed or struck down their anti-abortion laws in 1970, making legal abortion broadly available roughly three years before the rest of the country. On January 22, 1973, the Supreme Court's ruling in Roe v. Wade legalized abortion nationwide. The number of legal abortions rose sharply, from under 750,000 in 1973 to over 1.6 million by 1980, with substantial cross-state variation in abortion rates. Abortion was disproportionately used by teenagers, unmarried women, and economically disadvantaged women—groups whose children, prior research suggests, face elevated risks of adverse early-life circumstances and later criminal involvement. The staggered timing of legalization across states and persistent cross-state differences in abortion rates create variation in the exposure of subsequent birth cohorts to legalized abortion as they reach high-crime ages roughly 15-25 years later.
